summary: FCFS SAVI is a mechanism for source address validation in IPv6 networks. The first node to use a locally assigned address is the one allowed to keep using it, and others are blocked. It complements ingress filtering to help detect and prevent source address spoofing.

eli5.summary: The first kid to sit in a seat gets it, and others cannot pretend to be that kid. It stops people faking who a message is from.

questions: how to prevent ipv6 source address spoofing
how does fcfs savi stop ipv6 address spoofing
what is the difference between trusted and validating ports
subtitle: How a switch can stop hosts on a local link from faking IPv6 source addresses, by letting the first claimant keep each address.

tldr.problem: Nothing stops a host on a local IPv6 link from sending packets with a source address that belongs to someone else, and ingress filtering only covers traffic that comes in from other networks.
tldr.mechanism: Switches or routers running FCFS SAVI bind each source address to the port where it was first seen, confirm that claim with Neighbor Discovery messages, and drop packets that arrive from a different port.
tldr.outcome: It requires no change to hosts and complements ingress filtering, but it is only as strong as its binding anchor (the switch port) and assumes hosts defend their own addresses.

today: RFC 6620 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves DHCP-assigned addresses to a separate mechanism and recommends SEND SAVI where Secure Neighbor Discovery is deployed.

sections.title: Scope and Design Constraints
sections.content:
FCFS SAVI (First-Come, First-Served Source Address Validation Improvement) checks that the source address of packets sent by hosts on the local link has not been spoofed. It looks only at local traffic, meaning packets a host sends with its own address. Transit traffic, forwarded by routers with other hosts' addresses, is out of scope and is left to ingress filtering as described in RFC 2827. The two techniques complement each other.

The design targets locally assigned IPv6 addresses, especially those from Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 4862). To be easy to deploy, it changes nothing on the host: it defines no new protocol and no new messages, and relies on existing ones. The FCFS SAVI function can sit in a router or in a Layer 2 bridge.
sections.eli5: The guard only checks kids sending their own notes inside one classroom. Notes coming in from outside the school are checked by someone else.

sections.title: Address Ownership and Binding Anchors
sections.content:
Ownership is defined by the first-come, first-served principle: the first host that claims a source address owns it until further notice. When an address is first used, the device creates state that binds the address to a binding anchor, which is Layer 2 information the device already has, such as the switch port. Later packets with that source address are checked against the same anchor.

A host may move to another port and keep its address. So the device uses Neighbor Discovery to test whether the host is still reachable at the old anchor. If not, the new location is accepted and a new binding is created. If it is still reachable there, packets from the new anchor are dropped.

A SAVI solution is no stronger than its anchor. A MAC address is easy to spoof, which could even open a new Denial-of-Service vector if non-compliant packets are dropped, so this specification says only switch ports MUST be used as binding anchors.
sections.eli5: The first kid to sit in a seat gets a name tag stuck to that seat. If a different kid sits there later, the teacher asks whether the first kid is still around before changing the tag.

sections.title: The Protection Perimeter and Port Types
sections.content:
FCFS SAVI is perimetrical. The FCFS SAVI devices form a protection perimeter and check every packet that crosses it; once inside, packets are not checked again. Each device only stores bindings for anchors on ports that face the untrusted, outside part of the topology, so the binding state is spread across devices instead of every device storing everything. Before creating a binding, a device sends a Neighbor Solicitation (NS) for the address. If any Neighbor Advertisement (NA) comes back, a binding must already exist elsewhere and none is created locally.

Ports come in two kinds. Validating Ports (VPs) get full FCFS SAVI processing and filtering. Trusted Ports (TPs) get none. Trusted Ports connect to other FCFS SAVI devices, to routers and to switches that lead only to trusted nodes. Hosts, and non-SAVI switches that have hosts behind them, hang off Validating Ports. The devices must form a connected perimeter, because packets that never cross it are not validated.
sections.eli5: Think of a fence around a playground with gates. Kids coming through a gate get checked, but once they are inside nobody checks them again.

sections.title: Prefixes and Traffic Handling
sections.content:
To tell local from transit traffic, the device keeps an FCFS SAVI Prefix List of on-link prefixes. It MUST support filling that list by manual configuration and by Router Advertisements seen on Trusted Ports, and it MUST send a Router Solicitation (with the unspecified source address) when it boots.

Packets from a Trusted Port are forwarded with no SAVI processing. Packets from a Validating Port are compared with the prefixes of the receiving interface. If the source is not in an on-link prefix, the packet is transit traffic and SHOULD be discarded (the device MAY send ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable, code 5, "Source address failed ingress/egress policy"). If it is on-link, local validation runs. Packets with the unspecified source address are forwarded, except for the Neighbor Solicitations used in Duplicate Address Detection (DAD).

Each binding entry records the IP address, the binding anchor (port), a lifetime, a status and a creation time. The device MUST also join the solicited-node multicast group of every address whose state is not NO_BIND, so it keeps receiving DAD messages even after a host moves.
sections.eli5: The guard first asks whether a note's return address is from this classroom. If it is not, the note is thrown out. If it is, the guard checks the seat chart.

sections.title: The Binding State Machine
sections.content:
Each address has one of five states in each device: NO_BIND (no binding), TENTATIVE (waiting while DAD runs), VALID (verified and used for filtering), TESTING_TP-LT and TESTING_VP (a binding being challenged).

When a first data packet or a DAD Neighbor Solicitation arrives on a Validating Port for an unbound address, the device sends DAD Neighbor Solicitations itself (by default two, spaced T_WAIT apart) through Trusted Ports only, records the port as the anchor, and enters TENTATIVE. It MUST NOT forward the data packets until the binding is verified, though it MAY drop or hold them. If a Neighbor Advertisement answers from a Trusted Port, the address is in use elsewhere and the binding is cleared. If the tentative lifetime runs out, the binding becomes VALID.

In VALID, packets from the bound port refresh the lifetime. A packet or DAD message from a different Validating Port triggers a test toward the old port and moves the binding to TESTING_VP. If the old port answers, the binding stays; if the lifetime expires without an answer, the anchor moves to the new port. A DAD message from a Trusted Port, or an expiring lifetime, moves the binding to TESTING_TP-LT. If the binding's own port answers or sends data, it returns to VALID; otherwise the binding is dropped back to NO_BIND. The RFC's own figure is a simplified version of this machine.
sections.eli5: A seat starts empty. When a kid sits down, the teacher waits a moment to see if anyone objects, then the seat is theirs. If someone else tries to sit there, the teacher asks the first kid whether they are still there.

sections.title: Port Configuration and Default Values
sections.content:
The configuration rules are firm. The FCFS SAVI realm MUST be connected. Ports to other FCFS SAVI devices MUST be Trusted Ports, as MUST ports to routers. Ports to untrusted hosts MUST be Validating Ports, and ports to legacy switches that have any untrusted host behind them MUST be Validating Ports too. A legacy switch chain with only other SAVI devices or routers behind it MUST be a Trusted Port. On a switch that supports customer VLANs, the implementation MUST behave as if it ran one FCFS SAVI process per VLAN.

The defaults are TENT_LT of 500 milliseconds, DEFAULT_LT of 5 minutes and T_WAIT of 250 milliseconds. Implementations MAY let them be changed, but tuning them is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Doors to the teachers' room and other guards are marked trusted. Doors to where the kids are get checked. The waiting times are just a few quick pauses and one longer one.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The device itself can be attacked. Sending many different source addresses makes it create state until it runs out of memory, so when the database is full it is RECOMMENDED to delete the entries with a higher creation time, keeping older entries. It is also RECOMMENDED to reserve memory for at least four bindings per port. The memory used to hold data packets MUST be limited. Because the device sends two DAD messages in answer to one, it could be used as an amplifier, so it MUST rate-limit the messages it generates, per port.

Residual threats remain. Anyone who can use the same binding anchor passes validation, for example hosts behind a legacy switch on one port can spoof each other. An attacker who stops a host from answering DAD can take over its binding. A compromised router can still send spoofed traffic.

For privacy, personally identifying information such as the MAC address MUST NOT be kept in the database except when an attack is involved, and binding anchor information MUST NOT be logged without an identified reason. With Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971), the RFC recommends SEND SAVI instead, because the device does not hold the keys needed to sign the DAD messages it must generate.
sections.eli5: A sneaky kid might try to fill up the teacher's notebook with fake names, so the teacher keeps the oldest names and limits how fast they answer. Names of well-behaved kids are not written down.
